claim: Voltage-gated sodium channels located in axon initial segments (AIS) trigger action potentials (AP) and play pivotal roles in the excitability of cortical pyramidal neurons.
source: Voltage-gated sodium channels located in axon initial segments (AIS) trigger action potentials (AP) and play pivotal roles in the excitability of cortical pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the role of sodium channels in the AIS.

claim: NaV1.2 and NaV1.6 channels have differential electrophysiological properties and distributions.
source: The differential electrophysiological properties and distributions of NaV1.2 and NaV1.6 channels lead to distinct contributions to AP initiation and propagation.
evidence: This statement draws on established knowledge about these channel subtypes.

claim: NaV1.6 at the distal AIS promotes AP initiation and forward propagation.
source: While NaV1.6 at the distal AIS promotes AP initiation and forward propagation, NaV1.2 at the proximal AIS promotes the backpropagation of APs to the soma.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and cited literature about channel distribution and function.

claim: NaV1.2 at the proximal AIS promotes the backpropagation of APs to the soma.
source: While NaV1.6 at the distal AIS promotes AP initiation and forward propagation, NaV1.2 at the proximal AIS promotes the backpropagation of APs to the soma.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and cited literature about channel distribution and function.

claim: The small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) pathway modulates Na+ channels at the AIS to increase neuronal gain.
source: Here, we show the small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) pathway modulates Na+ channels at the AIS to increase neuronal gain and the speed of backpropagation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) pathway modulates Na+ channels at the AIS to increase the speed of backpropagation.
source: Here, we show the small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) pathway modulates Na+ channels at the AIS to increase neuronal gain and the speed of backpropagation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SUMO does not affect NaV1.6.
source: Since SUMO does not affect NaV1.6, these effects were attributed to SUMOylation of NaV1.2.
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors and experimental observations in this study.

claim: SUMO effects on neuronal gain and backpropagation speed were attributed to SUMOylation of NaV1.2.
source: Since SUMO does not affect NaV1.6, these effects were attributed to SUMOylation of NaV1.2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of SUMO on channel subtypes and experimental data.

claim: SUMO effects were absent in a mouse engineered to express NaV1.2-Lys38Gln channels that lack the site for SUMO linkage.
source: Moreover, SUMO effects were absent in a mouse engineered to express NaV1.2-Lys38Gln channels that lack the site for SUMO linkage.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from the mutant mouse model.

claim: SUMOylation of NaV1.2 exclusively controls INaP generation.
source: Thus, SUMOylation of NaV1.2 exclusively controls INaP generation and AP backpropagation, thereby playing a prominent role in synaptic integration and plasticity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data showing SUMO effects on persistent sodium current.

claim: SUMOylation of NaV1.2 exclusively controls AP backpropagation.
source: Thus, SUMOylation of NaV1.2 exclusively controls INaP generation and AP backpropagation, thereby playing a prominent role in synaptic integration and plasticity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data showing SUMO effects on backpropagation velocity.

claim: SUMOylation of NaV1.2 plays a prominent role in synaptic integration and plasticity.
source: Thus, SUMOylation of NaV1.2 exclusively controls INaP generation and AP backpropagation, thereby playing a prominent role in synaptic integration and plasticity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known roles of backpropagation in synaptic plasticity and the experimental findings.

claim: Action potentials initiate in the axon initial segment (AIS) in cortical pyramidal cells.
source: In cortical pyramidal cells, as in many central nervous system (CNS) neurons, action potentials (APs) initiate in the axon initial segment (AIS), the proximal part of the axon where the neuronal membrane is not covered with a myelin sheath.
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: The AIS is the proximal part of the axon where the neuronal membrane is not covered with a myelin sheath.
source: In cortical pyramidal cells, as in many central nervous system (CNS) neurons, action potentials (APs) initiate in the axon initial segment (AIS), the proximal part of the axon where the neuronal membrane is not covered with a myelin sheath.
evidence: This is a definition based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The AIS is characterized by a specialized assembly of scaffolding proteins and voltage-gated channels with distinctive biophysical properties.
source: The AIS is characterized by a specialized assembly of scaffolding proteins and voltage-gated channels with distinctive biophysical properties (Bean, 2007; Rasband, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: APs propagate forward from the AIS into the axonal arbor, triggering neurotransmitter release from presynaptic terminals.
source: Classically, APs propagate forward from the AIS into the axonal arbor, triggering neurotransmitter release from presynaptic terminals.
evidence: This is established knowledge about action potential propagation.

claim: APs can propagate backward into the dendrites of cortical pyramidal cells.
source: APs can also propagate backward into the dendrites of cortical pyramidal cells, where they are proposed to play a role in synaptic plasticity by regulating synaptic strength and the coordination of synaptic inputs (Stuart and Sakmann, 1994; Markram et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Backpropagating APs are proposed to play a role in synaptic plasticity by regulating synaptic strength and the coordination of synaptic inputs.
source: APs can also propagate backward into the dendrites of cortical pyramidal cells, where they are proposed to play a role in synaptic plasticity by regulating synaptic strength and the coordination of synaptic inputs (Stuart and Sakmann, 1994; Markram et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Both initiation and propagation of APs are critically dependent on the distribution and properties of voltage-gated Na+ (NaV) channels in specific neuronal compartments.
source: Both initiation and propagation of APs are critically dependent on the distribution and properties of voltage-gated Na+ (NaV) channels in specific neuronal compartments (Stuart et al., 1997; Hu et al., 2009; Baranauskas et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Identifying signaling pathways that regulate the biophysical properties of neuronal NaV channels is key to understanding spike generation, propagation, and integration in cortical circuits.
source: Therefore, identifying signaling pathways that regulate the biophysical properties of neuronal NaV channels is key to understanding spike generation, propagation, and integration in cortical circuits (Cantrell et al., 1996; Cantrell and Catterall, 2001; Bender et al., 2012; Kole and Stuart, 2012; Yin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature and represents a rationale for the study.

claim: Central neurons express three primary NaV channels α-subunit isoforms: NaV1.1, NaV1.2, and NaV1.6 in mature neurons.
source: Central neurons express, to varying degrees, three primary NaV channels α-subunit isoforms. NaV1.1, NaV1.2, and NaV1.6 are found in mature neurons, while NaV1.3 channels are also found in the developing nervous system (Goldin et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: NaV1.3 channels are found in the developing nervous system.
source: Central neurons express, to varying degrees, three primary NaV channels α-subunit isoforms. NaV1.1, NaV1.2, and NaV1.6 are found in mature neurons, while NaV1.3 channels are also found in the developing nervous system (Goldin et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Each NaV isoform has a distinct spatiotemporal distribution.
source: Each NaV isoform has a distinct spatiotemporal distribution and is subject to the activity of specific signaling pathways that regulate the biophysical properties and trafficking behavior of the channel.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sodium channel isoforms.

claim: Each NaV isoform is subject to the activity of specific signaling pathways that regulate the biophysical properties and trafficking behavior of the channel.
source: Each NaV isoform has a distinct spatiotemporal distribution and is subject to the activity of specific signaling pathways that regulate the biophysical properties and trafficking behavior of the channel.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sodium channel regulation.

claim: In mature pyramidal neurons, the AP trigger zone is located in the distal AIS.
source: For example, in mature pyramidal neurons, the AP trigger zone, which is located in the distal AIS, contains almost exclusively NaV1.6 channels (Lorincz and Nusser, 2008; Hu et al., 2009; Lorincz and Nusser, 2010; Tian et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The AP trigger zone in mature pyramidal neurons contains almost exclusively NaV1.6 channels.
source: For example, in mature pyramidal neurons, the AP trigger zone, which is located in the distal AIS, contains almost exclusively NaV1.6 channels (Lorincz and Nusser, 2008; Hu et al., 2009; Lorincz and Nusser, 2010; Tian et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: NaV1.6 channels are present in the nodes of Ranvier.

claim: The proximal portion of the AIS, soma, and dendrites is believed to contain mostly NaV1.2 channels.

claim: NaV1.6 channels activate at more negative voltages than other neuronal NaV isoforms in heterologous studies.
source: While heterologous studies show that NaV1.6 channels activate at more negative voltages than other neuronal NaV isoforms and have a higher propensity to generate non-inactivating currents, differences in the gating behavior of NaV1.2 and NaV1.6 channels appear to be subtle within their native neuronal milieu (Smith et al., 1998; Zhou and Goldin, 2004; Rush et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: NaV1.6 channels have a higher propensity to generate non-inactivating currents in heterologous studies.
source: While heterologous studies show that NaV1.6 channels activate at more negative voltages than other neuronal NaV isoforms and have a higher propensity to generate non-inactivating currents, differences in the gating behavior of NaV1.2 and NaV1.6 channels appear to be subtle within their native neuronal milieu (Smith et al., 1998; Zhou and Goldin, 2004; Rush et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Differences in the gating behavior of NaV1.2 and NaV1.6 channels appear to be subtle within their native neuronal milieu.
source: While heterologous studies show that NaV1.6 channels activate at more negative voltages than other neuronal NaV isoforms and have a higher propensity to generate non-inactivating currents, differences in the gating behavior of NaV1.2 and NaV1.6 channels appear to be subtle within their native neuronal milieu (Smith et al., 1998; Zhou and Goldin, 2004; Rush et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: NaV1.6 channels were not required to determine the initiation site for APs within the AIS.
source: Indeed, using knockout mice, we found that NaV1.6 channels were not required to determine the initiation site for APs within the AIS, for backpropagation into the dendrites, or for the lower activation threshold voltage for APs that is commonly observed in pyramidal neurons (Katz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors using knockout mice.

claim: NaV1.6 channels were not required for backpropagation into the dendrites.
source: Indeed, using knockout mice, we found that NaV1.6 channels were not required to determine the initiation site for APs within the AIS, for backpropagation into the dendrites, or for the lower activation threshold voltage for APs that is commonly observed in pyramidal neurons (Katz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors using knockout mice.

claim: NaV1.6 channels were not required for the lower activation threshold voltage for APs that is commonly observed in pyramidal neurons.
source: Indeed, using knockout mice, we found that NaV1.6 channels were not required to determine the initiation site for APs within the AIS, for backpropagation into the dendrites, or for the lower activation threshold voltage for APs that is commonly observed in pyramidal neurons (Katz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors using knockout mice.

claim: NaV1.6 channels are less sensitive to inhibition by cAMP-dependent protein kinase or protein kinase C-mediated phosphorylation.
source: Thus, NaV1.6 channels are less sensitive to inhibition by cAMP-dependent protein kinase or protein kinase C-mediated phosphorylation (Chen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: The differential sensitivity of NaV1.6 to phosphorylation explains divergent regulation of NaV channel subtypes following the activation of D1/D5 dopamine or 5-HT1A serotonergic receptors.
source: This finding explains divergent regulation of NaV channel subtypes following the activation of D1/D5 dopamine or 5-HT1A serotonergic receptors (Maurice et al., 2001; Yin et al., 2017).

claim: Ion channels are subject to post-translational regulation by covalent linkage of small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) proteins.
source: We have shown that ion channels are also subject to post-translational regulation by covalent linkage of small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) proteins (Rajan et al., 2005; Plant et al., 2010; Plant et al., 2011; Plant et al., 2012; Plant et al., 2016; Xiong et al., 2017; Plant et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature from the authors' previous work.

claim: Three SUMO isoforms (SUMO1–3) are operative in central neurons.
source: Three SUMO isoforms (SUMO1–3) are operative in central neurons and can modulate the gating of specific channels following their conjugation to the ε-amino group of specific lysine residues on the intracellular termini or cytoplasmic loops of the channel subunits.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SUMO isoforms.

claim: SUMO can modulate the gating of specific channels following their conjugation to the ε-amino group of specific lysine residues on the intracellular termini or cytoplasmic loops of the channel subunits.
source: Three SUMO isoforms (SUMO1–3) are operative in central neurons and can modulate the gating of specific channels following their conjugation to the ε-amino group of specific lysine residues on the intracellular termini or cytoplasmic loops of the channel subunits.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SUMO mechanism of action.

claim: The enzymes required to activate, mature, and conjugate SUMO reside in the plasma membrane of Xenopus oocytes, tissue culture cells, and neurons.
source: Further, we found the enzymes required to activate, mature, and conjugate SUMO reside in the plasma membrane of Xenopus oocytes, tissue culture cells, and neurons (Rajan et al., 2005; Plant et al., 2010; Plant et al., 2011; Plant et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature from the authors' previous work.

claim: SUMOylation is a dynamic process subject to rapid reversal by the action of the SENP family of sentrin-specific cysteine proteases.
source: Although SUMOylation is a covalent post-translational modification, it is a dynamic process subject to rapid reversal by the action of the SENP family of sentrin-specific cysteine proteases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SUMO regulation.

claim: SUMOylation increases excitability by decreasing potassium flux through KV and K2P channels.
source: Thus far, we have observed that SUMOylation increases excitability either by decreasing potassium flux through KV and K2P channels or by increasing the activity of NaV channels and that the opposite functional effects are mediated by the activity of SENPs.

source: Further, we have observed that SUMOylation status varies among channel types at baseline and in response to environmental stimuli such as hypoxia (Plant et al., 2016; Xiong et al., 2017; Plant et al., 2020), and particularly germane to this study, that SUMO has differential effects on the principal NaV channel isoforms expressed in central neurons.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature from the authors' previous work.

claim: SUMOylation status varies among channel types in response to environmental stimuli such as hypoxia.
source: Further, we have observed that SUMOylation status varies among channel types at baseline and in response to environmental stimuli such as hypoxia (Plant et al., 2016; Xiong et al., 2017; Plant et al., 2020), and particularly germane to this study, that SUMO has differential effects on the principal NaV channel isoforms expressed in central neurons.

claim: SUMOylation modulates the voltage-dependent gating of NaV1.2 channels via linking to lysine 38.
source: Specifically, we found that SUMOylation modulates the voltage-dependent gating of NaV1.2 channels via linking to lysine 38, but SUMO does not interact with NaV1.6 (Plant et al., 2016).

claim: SUMO does not interact with NaV1.6.

evidence: This is supported by cited literature from the authors' previous work.

claim: SUMO1 increases excitability via a synergistic effect on subthreshold K+ and Na+ conductances.
source: By combining whole-cell recordings with high-speed fluorescence imaging to simultaneously monitor Na+ flux in different subcellular compartments of L5 cortical neurons, we found that SUMO1 increases excitability via a synergistic effect on subthreshold K+ and Na+ conductances.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: SUMOylation suppresses the open probability of K+ channels.
source: Thus, SUMOylation suppresses the open probability of K+ channels while concurrently increasing Na+ influx via a leftward shift in the steady-state activation of subthreshold persistent Na+ currents.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: SUMOylation increases Na+ influx via a leftward shift in the steady-state activation of subthreshold persistent Na+ currents.
source: Thus, SUMOylation suppresses the open probability of K+ channels while concurrently increasing Na+ influx via a leftward shift in the steady-state activation of subthreshold persistent Na+ currents.

claim: SUMO effects on K+ and Na+ channels are absent in a CRISPR-generated mouse that constitutively expresses NaV1.2-Lys38Gln channels.

claim: NaV1.2-Lys38Gln is a channel variant that cannot be SUMOylated.

evidence: This is based on previous work showing that lysine 38 is the SUMO conjugation site.

claim: SUMOylation of NaV1.2 regulates the velocity of backpropagation in cortical pyramidal neurons independent of the speed at which AP propagate forward from the AIS.
source: Confirming the long-held notion for their roles in the AIS based on distribution, and consistent with our previous report that SUMO regulates NaV1.2 but not NaV1.6 channels, we demonstrate that SUMOylation of NaV1.2 regulates the velocity of backpropagation in cortical pyramidal neurons independent of the speed at which AP propagate forward from the AIS.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.
